A word of warning: Many (most?) MA schools are belt farms. It's about the only way to make any money and regardless of how noble the founder's intentions are when they start out, inevitably it becomes a numbers game driven by cheap labor (senior students do a lot of the teaching). There's nothing wrong with this per se however there are some really really horrible schools out there. Until you learn some good technique you really have no way to judge, so I always recommend that you find someone who's been doing MA for a while and ask them to accompany you to the schools you're considering. My acid test is the Turning Kick. Seems simple but proper execution is something that needs to be taught correctly until it becomes second nature. In my experience none of the Dojos that spring up at the malls teach this kick correctly (I'm looking at you Sung Lee). What is more the students are generally on a schedule of belt testing that is followed rigorously regardless of skills acquired. 14 YOs with BBs teaching class is NOT a sign that the school is better or even good. And did I mention that they charge for belt testing?

The more flamboyant, out spoken, and dismissive of other clubs and styles the founder is is also a good indication of a belt farm. These guys are good at promoting themselves first, everything else is secondary.

Don't let my comments put you off. It's a great time and you will meet some truly talented and inspiring people. Just keep eyes open going in. And don't hesitate to change schools if you begin to have doubts.

If you'd like, here's a brain teaser but you may have already heard this one:

There are 12 people on an island. Eleven of the people weigh the exact same and the last one weighs slightly more or slightly less. There is also a see-saw on the island but it can only be used three times before it breaks. How do you determine which person is of the different weight?

Also, Voaters, don't go posting the answer, please. I'm sure many of you know where this is from and probably have the answer already in mind.

How big is the see-saw? Can we just split the group in 2 to see which group of 6 is the heaviest? Then of that heavier group split it again into two groups of 3? Then the heavier group of three split again? Of the last three if the two you put on the see-saw even out you know the one standing is heaviest (or if one on the see-saw is heavier it would be obvious).
The see-saw can hold all of them if necessary. If you do an even weigh, it won't work every time unless you get lucky. Even then, keep in mind that the outlier may be slightly lighter OR heavier.

To get you started, it's good to establish a control group. I can tell you right now the first use of the see-saw shouldn't be an equal one. By that I mean your first group shouldn't be 6v6 as it can't establish which group has the heavier or the lighter outlier.
If they all weigh the same except one than wouldn't it be obvious when one side is higher than the other?

If you weight 6 v 6 and one side is heavier, then which side has the outlier who is either heavier or lighter than the rest?

1-6 v 7-12 Outcome : 1-6 is heavier

1-3 v 4-6 Outcome : Equal

Now you've established that 1-6 actually weigh the same, meaning the outlier is lighter and not present in the 1-6 group. However, you've used two of the three chances obtaining this information. This means you have one chance left to find out who is lighter. You're also left with the knowledge that the lighter outlier is present in group 7-12. You will be unable to use your last chance to identify the outlier since you've been left with 6 individuals.

What makes this problem especially difficult is the fact that you don't begin with the knowledge of what the outlier actually weighs. Are they heavier than the rest or lighter? If you knew this prior to the problem then a 6v6 split could work. It isn't impossible to find the answer but it is a bit of a thinker. I must admit that when I was presented with this problem it took me many hours to solve.
